analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Morning in Rendell Baker and others against Sandra Cohn. Mr. Carroll, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. T. Justice, it may please report. The question in these two consolidated cases is whether an ostensibly private school, which is retained by the state to discharge the state's obligation to provide special education, acts under color of law when it dismisses several of its teachers for criticizing the manner in which that education is provided. Petitioners are six former teachers and counselors at Respondent New Prospective School in Brookline, Massachusetts. They allege they were dismissed for fulfilling their professional duty to speak out on school matters affecting the education of their students. Although the school is ostensibly private, all 50 of its students were placed there by state agencies or local school committees under the Massachusetts Special Education Statute. Each child's educational program was prescribed by public officials. State agencies or local school committees also paid each child's tuition, with the result that as much as 99% of the school's operating funds were derived from public sources. Thus, the school had no students except those which had been placed there by public officials. It had virtually no operating funds except those which had been provided by public officials. It was contractually obligated to implement educational programs prescribed by public officials, and it had no function except to discharge the Commonwealth's own obligation to provide special education to students which public officials had placed at the school. Who owns the building and properties? The building and properties are privately owned by the school's trustees. Who selects the teachers? Teachers are selected by the school management, including the directors and the executive director of the school. Are any of them public officials? No. Under the circumstances of this case, petitioners submit that the school is subject to the same constitutional obligations as an ordinary public school in connection with the performance of its educational activities. To place the issue into its proper context, it is important to understand more fully the statutory scheme under which special education is provided in Massachusetts. Chapter 766 of the Acts of 1972 confers upon every school-aged child a statutory right to receive suitable, publicly funded education. If a child is suspected of having special learning needs, he is evaluated by a team of educators, physicians, and psychologists appointed by the state. If the team determines that the child does have special learning needs, then it formulates an individualized educational plan, or IEP, to meet those needs. The IEP establishes educational objectives for the child, and sets out in detail an educational program designed to achieve those objectives. By law, the IEP must be implemented by the child's regular public school to the fullest extent possible. If the regular public school is unable to implement the IEP, then but only then may the school committee place the child in a specially accredited private school, such as the respondent in this case. The school must agree to implement the IEP and to submit to extensive state regulation and inspection. It must also report periodically on the child's progress, with a view toward returning him to the public school as soon as possible. For its part, the school committee must pay each child's tuition, and it also must monitor the child's progress and the school's performance. The school committee also has an ongoing obligation to revise the child's IEP as the need arises. If the regular public school is unable to implement the IEP, and if the school committee is unable to locate a suitable private school which is willing and able to do so, then by law, the school committee must establish a suitable program of its own. So, in short, every school-age child has an unconditional right to suitable education, and the Commonwealth has an absolute duty to provide it. It's also significant that school attendance was made compulsory under Chapter 766 for children entitled to special educational benefits. This, then, was the statutory scheme under which state agencies or local school committees provided the school with all of its students and virtually all of its operating funds. Did the Court of Appeals for the First Circuit agree with all of your positions as to the statutory law of Massachusetts? I don't know of any disagreement that they expressed with any of these positions. The dismissals which gave rise to the litigation were all alleged to have been in retaliation for a petitioner's speech critical of school policies and administration. It was against this background and on these facts, which, as I've noted, the First Circuit assumed to be true for purposes of its opinion, that petitioners maintain that the school is subject to the same constitutional obligations as an ordinary public school in connection with the performance of its educational activities. Well, isn't that true? Of every private school, it must meet state standards? We think that there is a critical difference in this case. An ordinary private school is not discharging an obligation of the Commonwealth or of a state when it provides education, because the children who attend that school have chosen to reject the education which the state is required to offer. The school in this case was clearly discharging an obligation of the Commonwealth, not only in the sense that the Commonwealth was paying for the education and had prescribed the educational program for the child, but that the Commonwealth would have had to provide this education itself. These were children who had come forward to claim the special educational benefits which the state was statutorily obligated to provide. We contend that the school is subject to constitutional obligations on two principal grounds. Well, let me ask you, you say there's a great difference between the situation and the situation that Chief Justice posed to you, but isn't this state by statute required to furnish an education for everybody? Yes, it is required to furnish an education. If somebody wants to go to public school, he has a right to go to public school. Yes. By statute. Yes. And if he chooses to go to private school instead, why, that is at least a replacement for a state obligation, isn't it? It's a substitute for a state obligation as long as the state approves it as an adequate substitute. It is a substitute for the obligation of the child. Well, how is that different from this situation other than for the financing? Because the private school in that case is providing education to children who have, either they or their parents, have chosen to reject the public education which the state provides. Well, I know that that may be one way of talking about it, but it nevertheless is discharging a state obligation in both cases. Well... At least it's a substitute for a state obligation. It is a substitute, but I... Furthermore, the child is discharging his obligation in the same way in both cases. That is correct. The child is discharging his obligation to attend a school. And the state is... The state is relieved of an obligation in both cases. Well, the state would still have an obligation... Or is relieved of an obligation to do it itself. That is correct. That is correct. The important point that we wish to emphasize is that when the school provides education, in this case to these children, it is discharging an obligation of the state and performing a sovereign function as an agent or instrumentality of the Commonwealth. When state agencies or state employees provide services in discharge of the Commonwealth's obligation, they, of course, must observe constitutional standards when they do so. The question, then, in this case is whether a different standard should apply when the state elects to deliver those same services through a closely controlled agent like the school rather than through its own full-time employees. We maintain that the same standard must apply in either case because states should not have it within their discretion to avoid constitutional obligations by the simple expediency of farming out their statutory obligations. The existence or non-existence of constitutional rights must not be permitted to turn upon formal distinctions between agents who are on the state payroll and those who aren't. If states are permitted to retain altered egos like the school to deliver essential services, and if those altered egos are as free to disregard constitutional rights as the state chooses to permit them to be, then citizens will ultimately be dependent upon nothing more than the will of the state. Well, suppose a city has an obligation to provide roads and streets and bridges and things like that, which it does, and it contracts with a construction firm to build a bridge. It certainly has standards that they have to live up to. They put out for bids and they have the specifications, and they agree to pay a certain amount of money. They finance the entire deal. Do you think that that makes that independent contractor a state instrumentality for purposes of the 14th Amendment? Not necessarily. We would distinguish cases in which the private entity is performing a function on behalf of the state from situations in which it is not, and we would distinguish it on the basis of whether or not the private entity's conduct substantially and materially affects the delivery of the particular service, so that under this functional analysis... Well, suppose the fellow in charge of Bill, the superintendent of the job is fired. He's been in charge, and midway through the building of the bridge, he gets discharged for a reason that he says violates his due process rights. And he... And I would not be as... have as much of an impact on the delivery of the state services as the discharge in this case. I don't believe so. I think the distinction is that when a school fires teachers for fulfilling a professional duty to speak out on professional matters, on educational matters affecting students, that there is not only the immediate impact of losing those particular teachers, but that all teachers at that school then and in the future know that they risk dismissal for expressing those types of professional opinions. The president of Justice White's hypothetical employee working on this bridge spoke up and said that the company was not building the bridge correctly and that it might endanger the public. In most cases... Would that be any different? In most cases, I would say, yes, it would be different. Well, he's speaking out to protect the public. Unless... He thinks he's speaking out to protect the public. Unless that particular individual has a position of responsibility which... under which it is his job in discharging the obligation of the state in this case to say what he's saying. He's hired to build a bridge, not to talk. That's... If he is the superintendent of the job, that is correct. But if you take, for example, a truck driver or somebody who is laying the concrete and is criticizing the design of the bridge and is speaking in public forums, I would say that the private contracting company would have a right to discharge that individual because the... Would that be the superintendent, do you think? If the... If it is the superintendent's position to express opinions concerning the safety of the project, then in that case, I would say that he would have a right to speak out to the same extent that the state engineer in charge of the project would have a right to do so. Mr. Carroll, this is not a state institution, is it? It is... It is a private institution. Yes, Your Honor. And the employees are not state employees? They are not employees of the state. They are not on the state. Where did they get under... How did they get under the 14th Amendment? They are acting under the color of law in the sense that they are agents or instrumentalities. How are they agents? They're not paid by the state, are they? They are... They are not on the state payroll. They're... They weren't hired by the state, were they? They were not hired by the state. Well, how do they become state officials? They are paid by funds provided by the state and they are subject to the control of the state. The state has to... Harvard's too, isn't it? Excuse me? There are some people at Harvard that are paid with federal funds too, aren't they? But they are not discharging... And that's still private, isn't it? That is still private. They are not discharging any obligation of the Commonwealth to deliver the educational services which they are delivering. I just don't understand how they become state employees. They don't become state employees. But they aren't data's in quotes. They become instrumentalities of the state. And I think you need those quotes to get under the 14th Amendment. Well, as the... As the court... So tell me, persuade me I'm wrong. As the court said in Evans v. Newton, and this is the quote from the opinion, when private individuals or groups are endowed by the state with powers or functions governmental in nature, they become agencies or instrumentalities of the state and subject to its constitutional limitations. Now, there have been several opinions by this court in which private entities have been held subject to constitutional obligations. For example, in Burton v. Wilmington Parking Authority, the Eagle Coffee Shop was, of course, private. Did that case say that the employees were state employees? They weren't even involved. The employees weren't involved in the case. No. That case said that the... Well, I'm still waiting for one that'll help you. They become... I think that's your problem. They are not state employees, but I don't believe the 14th Amendment requires or applies only to employees. I believe that it applies to persons who are acting under color of law, and that when the private employee is discharging an obligation of the common law... Suppose the private employee makes his speech to a private student, would that be protected by the 14th Amendment? Under the circumstances in which it would... If under the circumstances... I gave you the circumstances. In the school, he got a group of private students who were paying their tuition and told them... Made a speech to them. Is that a protected speech? If these were private students who had not been sent there by the common law, the answer is no. It would be a private speech. That's not it. Well, what was this speech made to? Only public students? There were no students at this school except students who had been sent by state agencies or local school committees. All 50 of the students had been placed there by the state. Was that done after? Was that school open before the statute or after? There isn't anything in the record about the history of the school. I believe it was opened shortly before the statute. And I don't know if there's anything... I believe there's nothing in the record as to whether it ever had any students except those placed by the state. Well, you go down all of the indicia of a state employee and they don't have any. Did they take an oath to the state? They did not take an oath but they signed a contract which provided that they would discharge the obligation of the commonwealth to implement the IEV. And so did Bugle to sign contracts too, wasn't it? Excuse me? The fact they signed a contract doesn't have anything to do with my point. Well, did they sign a contract with the state? Yes, with the local school committees and state agencies. Agents of the state or instrumentalities of the state, state agencies. They filed a contract to teach and to be paid. Did they file it with the school or the school board? I mean the school. Perhaps I misunderstood your honest question. I thought you did. The school itself signs a contract with the state agencies. The state didn't have anything to do with it. The state is a, they are completely different groups of people. They are different groups of people but the state is responsible for the students being there and it's responsible for the school's existence. If I may draw an analogy to other decisions by this court, for example, Williams v. United States reported at 341 U.S. Reports was a case where a private security policeman was held subject to constitutional obligations in a criminal case, the counterpart of the civil statute involved here, because he was acting under a license by the state and he beat up a group of private employees. Which license gave them right to carry a gun and kill somebody. Well, the, Well, that's, that's, what do, what do these teachers have from the state? What license, if any? They were specially accredited, they were accredited by the state to teach but that does not distinguish them from ordinary public school teachers. However, in order to teach in the new prospective school or other accredited schools, you must receive the same comparable certification to public school teachers, which is a higher certification than the certification required. Isn't it true for all private schools? No, it is not. Really? The certification with one state it is, right? Some states have the same certification. I, I don't know the answer to that. I would not be surprised. But in Massachusetts, the certification requirements are now higher for special education teachers in private schools than for ordinary teachers. Now, Mr. Carroll, even if the school is acting in a sovereign role as to the students, how can you argue that the school is acting in a sovereign role with regard to its personnel policies? Where is the nexus for personnel policy? The nexus comes from the fact that it is the function of providing education which is important here. Under, under what we would maintain this functional approach to be, the school should be subject to the same constitutional obligations as an ordinary public school to the extent its conduct has a material effect on the delivery of the service and firing... Mr. Carroll, it is a concern because a number of cities and counties and governmental units in the country are contracting with private employers, if you will, to perform certain functions, for example, fire protection or garbage pickup services. This is a rather widespread practice around the country. Under your theory, then, all of these employees of these private contractors with a city or a county would now be considered to be engaged in state action. Is that right? State action for some purposes, not necessarily all purposes. That would be state action only to the extent that the challenged conduct had a material effect on the delivery of the service so that there might well be instances where the private security police, for example, or the private firemen would not be subject to constitutional obligations. They would only be in connection with those activities which the private citizen who is receiving the benefit of that service will expect will have a material effect on the quality of the service itself. Now, in this... But under your theory, I take it any labor management dispute in the company that was providing the trash service or the fire protection service would affect the delivery of the service since you're basically dealing with a labor management dispute here at the New Perspective School. I think what is more important than the particular episode is whether a rule of law which says that the private entity may do something or other might have the effect on the future delivery of that service. For example, if we take a case of a private maintenance company which is plowing city streets, I think that if the maintenance company plowed the streets in the minority ethnic neighborhoods last over and over, that that conduct is clearly affecting the quality of the delivery of the service and it should be subject to a constitutional obligation. However, when that same maintenance company makes decisions about who it's going to hire or what equipment it's going to buy or who it's going to buy equipment from, the impact on the quality of the service is substantially less. And that's why I come back in this case to the point that if teachers know that they may be discharged for expressing professional opinions about the quality of education, then the quality of education will seriously suffer. Well, what if one of several supervisors of a private fire company that's employed by a city to furnish fire protection services makes a statement to the press that this organization is poorly run from top to bottom and follows antiquated fire protection procedures and we ought to get rid of top management? Well, I think that this is similar to the question before about the bridge supervisor. If this person is simply an individual who is expressing his own opinions and is not in a position which confers upon him the responsibility to express opinions of that type, then when he is discharged for expressing such opinions, the company discharging him is exercising a private function, is performing a private function because this particular individual's speech is probably not any significantly more important than any other individual speech in so far as that quality of service is concerned. And you do have to separate the functions of the private entity which are private from the functions of the private entity which are public. I think the state action requirement, the primary purpose, is to protect a zone of privacy, to establish a zone of privacy. And it is the sensitive balancing of interest which is involved here. You would have a, I would think, a stronger case if there had been some express permission. Say a state statute said you may fire any of your people without a hearing, without losing your grant, without losing your, and the school have fired somebody without a hearing. I think. But there isn't even that here, is there? No, what there is is an abdication of responsibility. And I think that that is akin to the situation you had in the so-called white primary cases, where the Democratic Party, particularly, for example, in Terry v. Adams, was not retained by the state to determine voter eligibility requirements in general elections. But the state, in effect, abdicated responsibility to the party to permit it to determine eligibility requirements in the only elections which counted, namely the Democratic pre-primaries. So that in that case, the party was held subject to constitutional obligations to the extent the state permitted it to perform that function. So that I think abdication of responsibility, or as in this case, an express delegation of responsibility, is a substitute for the kind of regulatory involvement that the court has dealt with from time to time, where the private entity is ordered to do something. We are certainly not dealing with a case where a private entity has been ordered to do something. We are dealing with a case where the state has expressly retained the private entity to discharge an obligation of the state to provide an essential service. Mr. Carroll, would your argument be the same if this particular school had only one or two students out of the public sector for which the state is paying? In that case, I think we would acknowledge that the school would be performing a dual function. To the extent it is providing education to those one or two students, certainly it is discharging a public obligation, but it is also performing a private obligation. The parents who send their children to that school voluntarily do have a right, an important right, to have those children taught in a manner and by people that they are comfortable with. I think that to the extent you can separate the dual nature of the function, you should do so. For example, I think it would be unconstitutional for the school you describe to threaten one student with dismissal for writing a letter to a local paper. What about this case? If the school had only one student publicly funded, would you think that your regulatory argument would stand up here? I think in that case you would have to say which function predominates it. In that case, I would say the private function predominates. I would say that the likelihood is in that case that the school had taken that one student more as an accommodation to the state in order to provide for its own continued existence. And that would be a different case than the one we have here, where the school obviously was depending upon the state for its very existence because all of its students were provided by the state. I would like to reserve the balance of my time. Excuse me. Do they get any private money? Or is it in the record? I think there were two years covered in the discovery. In one year, it was about 9%. In the second year, it was 1% of operating funds. I don't know what the endowment is of the school. I don't believe that's in the record. But in the second year with which this case is concerned, 99% of the operating funds were provided by the state. Thank you. Mr. Feinberg. Thank you. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. The New Prospective School is a private, autonomous, independent private school. It retains all of the essential characteristics of a private school. Nothing in its operation or in the operation of the Massachusetts Special Education Statute, Chapter 766, alters the essential private nature of that school. The school was incorporated in 1971. Most private schools don't get 99% of their funds from the state, either. That is correct, Your Honor. The fact, however, that the school gets that kind of money through the state in no way alters the essential private characteristics of the school. That is to say, with regard to who goes to the school, who teaches at the school, and what the teachers teach at the school, the school itself, and only the school, retains the decision-making authority. You mean the State Board of Education has no jurisdiction over the school at all? The State Board of Education has regulatory authority. I thought so. But it does not have direct control in the sense that it does not have any control over the decision-making powers of the school in its day-to-day operation, who it hires, who it fires, and indeed, who even goes to the school. Well, did you suggest that the students are selected only by the school and not assigned by the state? That is absolutely correct, Your Honor. What happens in the admission policy of the school is as follows. A referring public agency, such as a school committee, will send over to the school the child and usually, in fact, always the child's parents. An interview is arranged. A certain amount of testing is accomplished. And at that point, what is known as the individual educational plan is developed. That plan is looked at by the school and a decision is made whether or not to admit that child to the school. The school may at that... Is that the school committee? I'm sorry? Is that the school committee? That is not the school committee, Your Honor. What does the school committee do? All the school committee does. The ultimate response... The last responsibility of the school committee is to refer a child whom they have deemed to be to be qualified for a private placement outside of the public school system. And that is a public committee, not a private committee. The referral itself is the public function of the school committee. The decision... Pursuing state law. That is correct. Under the end of the chapter. Pursuing state law. That is correct. The decision, however, of whether or not to accept that child rests with the school. And if the child is rejected, how does the state, or the school board, discharge its obligation to provide special education? It must discharge its obligation by referring that child to another school, and another school whereby that child's individual educational plan is more consonant with that other school. And if this process ends up that no other school will take the child, then how is the child at the time? Then the public school must establish its own program for the school within the public school system. There is no... There is an obligation upon the public school system to do something for that child. But it is not necessarily so that the child must go to the New Prospective School or any other privately operated institution. Actually, in the two years involved here, how many of the children at New Prospective School were referred by some public school board? I believe the percentages were... Well, it was over 80%. Forty-three students were referred by public school systems. Seven students came through other state agencies. The other state agencies, Your Honor, were the department... Were there any of them who had not been referred by some state agency? Not in the two years in question, Your Honor. All 50 of these students were referred by some state agency. However, the school did have... How many referred children were rejected? The record is totally silent with regard to that, Your Honor. It is clear, however, that the school has the authority to reject students. It has the authority as well to admit private referrals that are outside of the system of special education within the Commonwealth. And in the two years in question, the record is again silent with regard to... It is not silent with regard to that. There were none in the two years in question with regard to that. Mr. Feinberg, putting Section 1981 and Runyon against McCrary on one side for the purpose of my question, do you think the school could consistently with the 14th Amendment in 1983 reject children on the basis of race? For these purposes, yes, Your Honor. Yeah. I would suggest to the court that for these purposes, this school is a private school and is protected by the First Amendment's right to free association and a right to pursue an independent educational policy, including that kind of discriminatory policy. Now, in addition to McCrary, there's also, of course, state law, which would preclude them in this instance from that kind of discrimination on the basis of race. And if there were such petitioners, they would have their remedy under state law. Do you rely at all on the fact that this is a teacher discharge case rather than a student rejection case? I'm not sure I understand the... Well, do you think the constitutional issue would be any different if the plaintiff were not a teacher who was denied employment for speaking out against the school policy, but rather were a child who had been denied admission because of his race or religion? I think, Your Honor, that it would be a... It would certainly be a different kind of a case in the sense that, at least with regard to the child, the entitlement program would certainly... It is directed toward providing services to the child, as the First Circuit distinguished the child from the teacher. But for purposes of the state action requirement, that threshold inquiry would be the same, Your Honor. And under that threshold inquiry, the argument of the respondents here would be that the school still would retain its private quality and it would make no constitutional difference. Well, putting perhaps the same question in a little different form, if the Wilmington parking case had not involved discrimination against a patron, but rather had been firing an employee or something, you'd say that case would still equally apply to a discharge of an employee? You don't think the Constitution draws any distinction based on the character of the claim, anyway, when you're analyzing the state action issue? No, not necessarily, Your Honor. What I would suggest, however, is that the Wilmington case is substantially different from this case in the sense that in the Wilmington case, we were talking about the closeness of the relationship between the entity and the state, whereas here the major argument of the petitioners is that there's been a delegation or a farming out, as Mr. Carroll indicated, of the function. And under that kind of analysis, the public function doctrine concept under Flagg Brothers and under the election cases, that kind of analysis would indicate that we would have to have here a delegation, a whole full delegation of the public function, a function that was exclusively given over to, in the state's hands. That is exactly the opposite of what we have here. In this instance, what we have is a situation in which, historically, the education of handicapped children has never been a public function. Historically, indeed, the education of such handicapped children has always been in private hands, and such children were routinely excluded from the public sector. Are you talking about the old 50 states? No, I'm talking about Massachusetts, Your Honor. You didn't say so. I'm sorry. My expertise and knowledge in this area is limited to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for these purposes. But within that context, the state has never entered into this field until the very recent past. And when it did, under Chapter 766, what it did was to encourage an outreach to the private sector, rather than incorporate it into its public school system. What it was doing here by establishing a special education program was to say, we cannot do it alone, and we establish an entitlement program whereby, if we can't do it, we will seek in every way we can to find an appropriate placement for a child in the private sector and pay for it. And that is exactly what has happened in this instance. Well, now I can see why the answer to Mr. Justice Stevens' question by you, you couldn't do that on race. I'm sorry, Your Honor. James Against Missouri says if you've got a school, you can't relegate the Negro to some other school. You have to let them in that school. So I see why he don't want to get the admission in there. But, Your Honor, even though I would suggest to the Court that when we talk about the discrimination cases, we are not talking about the same generic kind of case that this is. This is a state entitlement program that is neutral on its face. It is not a situation in which we are dealing at all with a discriminatory practice by the school with regard to the admission of students. And in that sense, we don't have to face any of the issues that are raised in those cases. Would you concede, Mr. Feinberg, that the school acts in the form of state action with respect to any function at all? I would not, Your Honor. I would not in the following sense. With regard to all of its essential functioning, and I've already gone through the admission practice, but in addition, with regard as well to its educational plan and with regard to its personnel practices, and I would suggest to the Court that those are the three major functions of any school, private or public, in terms of its decision-making authority, that the private board of directors and the privately employed staff of that school make those decisions.
